title: Profiling tooling and scripts runbook v5
content:
Overview:
This runbook describes the profiling tooling and scripts we use for serving-runtime performance investigations. It covers perf CI jobs (how we collect baseline runs in CI and store artifacts), flamegraph and trace collection scripts (CPU and GPU), trace collectors (bcc/bpftrace, perf, nvprof/Nsight), and triage/playbook steps for common bottlenecks. This is an iterative, working doc - v5 includes CI automation improvements and GPU capture conventions.

Goals:
- Make perf artifacts reproducible and shareable (standard file names, metadata).
- Provide CI-level regression detection for latency tail and p50/p95 throughput.
- Produce flamegraphs and trace captures that engineers can open locally.
- Have low-overhead collection modes for production (sampling) and high-fidelity for staging (instrumented).

Conventions and artifact naming:
- Artifact root: gs://redwood-perf-artifacts/<repo>/serving-runtime/<date>/<job-name>/<commit>-<run-id>/
- Key files per run (always present):
  - metadata.txt (json-ish but kept as single-line key=val entries)
  - cpu.perf.data (perf.data from `perf record`)
  - cpu.flame.svg (flamegraph generated from perf.data)
  - async-trace.json (async stack traces / tokio traces, if applicable)
  - gpu.nsys.qdrep (Nsight Systems capture) or gpu.nvprof (legacy)
  - kernel-trace.txt (optional, output of `bcc/execsnoop`/`trace-cmd`)
- Metadata fields to include in metadata.txt: commit, branch, job, docker image, command line, server type (cpu/gpu), model name, seq_len_distribution, input_batch, seed randomness flag.

Perf CI job (high-level):
- Trigger: nightly + PR that changes serving-runtime core.
- Runner: large instance with same HW SKU as Dedicated (at least one), or our performance emulator. For GPU captures, use machine with same NVIDIA driver stack (match prod).
- Steps:
  1) Checkout commit and build docker image with perf tooling installed (perf, FlameGraph repo, bcc, nsys CLI).
  2) Run warmup traffic for 3x typical p95 to populate caches/KV cache.
  3) Start tracing/monitoring collectors (see collector scripts below).
  4) Run load harness for configured duration (default 5m) capturing p50/p90/p95 latencies and token throughput.
  5) Save raw artifacts and generate derived visualizations (flamegraphs, nsys reports) and metrics.
  6) Upload artifacts to GCS and notify perf-dashboard.
  7) Compare new flamegraph/baseline using flame-diff script. If regression above threshold, post comment on PR and add ENG-xxxx ticket.

Example GH Actions snippet (simplified):
- name: Run perf job
  uses: docker://gcr.io/redwood-tools/perf-harness:latest
  with:
    args: ./run_perf_job.sh --model gpt-3-like --seq-len 512 --duration 300 --collectors perf,nsys,bcc

Key collector scripts (location: scripts/profiling/ in repo):
- collect/cpu_perf_record.sh
  - Usage: ./cpu_perf_record.sh <pid|command> <outdir>
  - runs: perf record -F 99 -g --call-graph dwarf -o $outdir/perf.data -- <command>
  - Notes: use -g --call-graph dwarf for async code; for JITed code we rely on frame pointers or map addresses to symbols via /proc/<pid>/maps + addr2line.

- collect/stackcollapse-perf.pl + flamegraph.pl pipeline:
  - perf script -i perf.data | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
  - ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > cpu.flame.svg
  - Keep uncollapsed `out.folded` for diffs.

- collect/async_stack_trace_collector.py
  - Polls the runtime via admin endpoint for sampled async stack traces (for tokio or async executors we instrument small sampler) -> writes async-trace.json (list of stacks with timestamp).

- collect/gpu_nsys_capture.sh
  - Usage: ./gpu_nsys_capture.sh <pid|docker-container> <outdir>
  - Runs: nsys profile -o $outdir/nsys --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=none --sample=cpu
  - Output: .qdrep and .sqlite; convert to .nsys-report via nsys UI or `nsys stats`. Keep full capture only for staging; for nightly CI we use condensed summary via nsys summary export.

- collect/bpftrace_async_hotspots.bt
  - A lightweight eBPF script to sample kernel/user stacks and attribute to PID/comm. Good for production with very low overhead. Example usage: sudo bpftrace bpftrace_async_hotspots.bt -o out/kern.txt

Flame-diff and automated comparisons:
- flame-diff tool compares folded stacks and highlights new hot paths. Pipeline:
  - Keep golden folded file for the canonical commit (store in gs://redwood-perf-golden/serving-runtime/<model>/<seq>/golden.folded)
  - New run produces run.folded -> run.folded.gz uploaded
  - Run: ./scripts/profiling/flame_diff.sh golden.folded run.folded > flame_diff_report.md
  - If run increases p95 or new hot functions appear above threshold, mark as regression.

Triage/playbook (when a regression is detected):
1) Confirm CI environment parity: image, CPU freq governor, driver versions, docker run flags (CPU pinning, hugepages, NUMA). Add metadata to run to capture those.
2) Check metrics: CPU utilization, context-switches, syscall counts (perf stat).
3) Look at flamegraph: focus on top 10 stacks by self time.
4) If race/lock suspected, collect lock contention traces (`perf lock` or `bcc` tools like `offcputime`).
5) For async stalls, inspect async-trace.json to find tasks with large wake-to-run latencies.
6) For GPU regressions: compare Nsight summaries for memcpy/launch times, check stream stalls, kernel queueing, and driver warnings.
7) Run binary-search: bisect commit range using perf CI to identify first bad commit.

Low overhead production sampling (recommended):
- Use eBPF-based sampler (bpftrace) that emits 1 sample/100ms aggregated per function; push aggregated counters to Prometheus. Keep raw captures only on-demand.
- Tag traces with request ID so we can correlate slow requests with stack samples.

Common pitfall checklist (notes-to-self style):
- Don't rely on perf with inlined JIT symbols unless symbolization step is validated. Use addr2line on release builds with separate debug symbols.
- Ensure docker image contains the same libc and glibc versions as prod for stack traces to match.
- For short-lived processes, `perf record` sometimes misses stacks; prefer `perf record -a -g` on the host for a short window or capture with `perf record` on the container PID with --vmlinux if available.
- Sampling frequency too high -> overhead; too low -> noisy flamegraphs. Start at 99Hz for CPU.

Quick commands (cheat sheet):
- Generate flame: perf record -F 99 -g --call-graph dwarf -o perf.data -- ./harness --args
  perf script -i perf.data | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
  ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > cpu.flame.svg
- Collect async stacks from runtime admin: curl http://localhost:8081/debug/async-stacks > async-trace.json
- Nsight capture (interactive): nsys profile --sample=cpu --trace=cuda,nvtx --output myrun ./run_harness
- bpftrace live hotspots: sudo bpftrace -e 'profile:hz:99 /pid==<pid>/ { @[ustack()] = count(); }' -o bpf.out

Onboarding checklist for new engineers:
- Read this runbook and run the quick commands in a staging harness.
- Make a small PR that adds a perf CI job for a toy harness and ensure artifacts are uploaded.
- Learn the FlameGraph workflow (stackcollapse -> flamegraph -> flame-diff).

Open items / TODOs:
- Add automated symbolization for stripped release binaries (build debug symbol artifacts and store alongside perf artifacts).
- Integrate Nsight summary exporter into perf CI so we get consistent JSON summaries rather than bulky qdrep files.
- Investigate using pprof-compatible traces for some async stacks so we can use existing pprof tools.
- Add automated correlation between trace IDs (from request logs) and perf artifacts in the perf dashboard.

Appendix: helpful links and references:
- FlameGraph repo: https://github.com/brendangregg/FlameGraph
- bcc tools: https://github.com/iovisor/bcc
- Nsight Systems: https://developer.nvidia.com/nsight-systems
- Example perf CI job: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/actions/workflows/perf.yml

Notes: This doc intentionally mixes polished instructions and quick scratch notes. Keep updating when adding new collectors or when we change the golden baseline process.
